lead: An aircraft left alone does not hold an altitude, a heading or a bank angle. It drifts with every gust and every change of thrust. A flight control system is the chain that lets a pilot, or later a computer, demand a motion and get it: a cockpit control moves, linkage carries the movement to a surface, the surface deflects into the airflow, airloads appear, and the aircraft rotates about one of its axes. The same chain runs from a Cessna 172R to an airliner, though the force source changes. See 1.3 for that step.

sections.h3: Six freedoms, three axes, three primary surfaces

blocks.text: An aircraft has six degrees of freedom: three translations (fore-aft, lateral, vertical) and three rotations. A degree of freedom is one independent way the body can move. A flight control system commands the rotations directly; translation follows from attitude and thrust.

items: Roll — rotation about the longitudinal axis, nose to tail. The ailerons move in opposite senses: the up-going aileron cuts lift on its wing and the down-going one raises it, so the aircraft banks.
Pitch — rotation about the lateral axis, wingtip to wingtip. The elevator sits on the horizontal tail; trailing edge up pushes the tail down and the nose up.
Yaw — rotation about the vertical axis. The rudder sits on the vertical tail; trailing edge left pushes the tail right and the nose left.

blocks.text: The ailerons also cause adverse yaw: the down-going aileron makes more drag and pulls the nose away from the turn. The rudder corrects it. Some syllabi call the aileron, elevator and rudder the primary controls.

A pilot commands a deflection, not a force. At speed a few degrees of surface produce a large moment; the linkage gearing sets how many millimetres of stick travel give one degree of surface. That ratio is the first design choice.

sections.h3: Secondary controls work on the wing or on the surface, not on the axis directly

items: Flaps: trailing-edge surfaces on the wing. Extending them raises lift and drag, so the aircraft can fly slower for take-off and landing.
Slats: leading-edge surfaces that extend to delay stall at a high angle of attack.
Spoilers: upper-surface wing panels that lift up to spoil lift and add drag. They are used for descent, as a speedbrake, and on some aircraft to help roll.

Trim tabs: small hinged tabs on a primary surface. Moving the tab changes the hinge moment, so the surface stays deflected with little or no stick force. The tab moves the surface; the surface moves the aircraft.
Throttle: not a surface, but part of the control chain because it sets thrust.

blocks.text: Some syllabi group these as auxiliary controls. Notice the difference: a primary control changes an axis of motion, while a secondary control changes the wing's lift or the surface's hinge moment.

sections.h3: The conventional chain, part by part

blocks.text: The Cessna 172R is a full mechanical single: a yoke on a column, two rudder pedals, a throttle lever and a manual trim wheel. No hydraulic boost sits between pilot and surface. Follow one demand: pull the yoke back, the column rotates, a rod moves forward, a bell crank changes the direction, cables run aft through pulleys, a turnbuckle sets tension, and a horn on the elevator converts cable pull into surface rotation about the hinge.

blocks.text: Rods and cables do the same job by different means; 1.2 compares them. The chain is sized by gearing. Too little gearing (only a few mm of stick travel per degree of surface) makes the aircraft twitchy and the stick forces high. Too much gearing makes the response sluggish: the pilot makes large stick movements and the forces feel light.

spec.aria: The pilot's demand passes through cockpit controls and mechanical linkage to a surface, whose airloads move the aircraft, and the pilot closes the loop by feel and sight.

examples.question: The elevator of a light aircraft moves 25° when the control column travels 120 mm from neutral. (a) Find the gearing in mm of column travel per degree of elevator. (b) The pilot pulls with 60 N and the linkage gives a mechanical advantage of 4 from grip to elevator push rod; find the push-rod force. (c) The elevator horn arm is 80 mm; find the hinge moment the rod produces.
steps: Gearing = column travel ÷ elevator angle = 120 mm ÷ 25° = 4.8 mm per degree.
Gearing and mechanical advantage are linked: gearing = mechanical advantage × horn arm (with consistent units). The numbers here are chosen for practice and need not match exactly.
Push-rod force = pilot force × mechanical advantage = 60 N × 4 = 240 N.
Assume the push rod acts at right angles to the horn arm; at an angle θ the moment is F × arm × sin θ. Convert the horn arm to metres: 80 mm = 0.08 m.
Hinge moment = push-rod force × horn arm = 240 N × 0.08 m = 19.2 N·m.
In a steady hold the rod moment equals the aerodynamic hinge moment; to move the surface the rod moment must be larger by the amount needed to accelerate the surface and its linkage.
examples.answer: Gearing is 4.8 mm per degree, push-rod force is 240 N, and the rod produces a hinge moment of 19.2 N·m.

traps: Putting roll on the rudder. The rudder yaws the aircraft; the ailerons roll it, and they also cause adverse yaw.
Saying a trim tab moves the aircraft. The tab moves the surface, and the surface moves the aircraft.
Mixing the axes: roll is about the longitudinal axis, pitch about the lateral axis, yaw about the vertical axis.
Using millimetres in a hinge-moment sum. Convert the horn arm to metres, so the answer is in N·m, not N·mm.
Thinking ailerons turn the aircraft directly. They bank it; the horizontal component of lift does the turning.

quiz.q: Name the three primary flight controls and the axis each rotates the aircraft about.
quiz.a: Aileron — roll, about the longitudinal axis. Elevator — pitch, about the lateral axis. Rudder — yaw, about the vertical axis.

quiz.q: Why does the down-going aileron produce adverse yaw?
quiz.a: It increases lift on its wing but also increases drag. That extra drag on the outer wing pulls the nose away from the intended turn, so the rudder or a differential aileron linkage is needed to correct it.

quiz.q: A control column moves 100 mm and the elevator moves 20°. Find the gearing in mm per degree.
A trim tab reduces the stick force needed to hold an elevator deflection. Does it change the aircraft's pitch attitude by itself? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The tab changes the hinge moment on the elevator, so the elevator can stay deflected with less force from the pilot or from the linkage. The elevator deflection then changes the tail lift and pitches the aircraft. The tab acts on the surface, not directly on the aircraft.
A pivoted lever in the linkage that changes the direction of rod or cable travel.

quiz.q: Why must cables run in matched pairs while a push-pull rod need not?
quiz.a: A cable can carry only a pull, so a second cable is needed to carry the return movement. A rod is stiff in both tension and compression, so one rod carries push and pull.

quiz.q: A push rod exerts 300 N on an elevator horn whose arm is 60 mm. Assume the push rod acts at right angles to the horn arm. Find the hinge moment.
quiz.a: Arm = 60 mm = 0.06 m. Hinge moment = 300 N × 0.06 m = 18 N·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the mechanical chain is the fallback layer inside fly-by-wire. The Airbus A320 family keeps a mechanical backup path to the rudder and to the pitch trim. Other fly-by-wire types differ: some have no such mechanical path. Search for "control loading system", "artificial feel unit" and "Cessna 172 control rigging" to see how the parts in the table are adjusted on a real aircraft. Newer light aircraft replace the cables with torque tubes and push rods, which reduces rigging error and maintenance. The vocabulary here — gearing, horn arm, hinge moment — is the same vocabulary used in the powered and fly-by-wire chapters that follow.
